label: Real CPU-only PyTorch training loop with asynchronous checkpoints; A/B/C comparison, fresh-process exactness, and SIGKILL resume. Synthetic seeded model/data, single host, no GPU, no fleet claim.

checkpoint.snapshot: clone of parameters, AdamW exp_avg/exp_avg_sq/step and the step counter

data.rule: seq[b,t] = (offset[b] + t) mod vocab; predict the next token

loop.description: explicit multi-head-attention transformer block stack (LayerNorm, GELU MLP, causal attention) trained with AdamW on a deterministic seeded synthetic next-token dataset
fixed: OMP/MKL/OPENBLAS/NUMEXPR thread counts forced to 1 before torch import
no dropout, no data augmentation, fixed batch order
single CPU host; no CUDA runtime in the court

losses: WeftFS total loop wall is 1.20x the torch.save file baseline (3577.8 ms vs 2982.6 ms).
WeftFS total loop wall is 1.14x the local PyTorch DCP baseline (3577.8 ms vs 3128.2 ms).
WeftFS synchronisation pause is 3.50x the DCP pause (2.85 ms vs 0.82 ms); the pause is the state clone plus submit, not the encode.
A WeftFS checkpoint completion is 22.06x the local DCP completion (445.9 ms vs 20.2 ms); it does not stall the loop but it needs a longer checkpoint interval to stay off the next checkpoint's path.
WeftFS checkpoint load on resume is 8.13x the local DCP load (182.1 ms vs 22.4 ms).
A WeftFS checkpoint completion is 118x the torch.save worker (445.9 ms vs 3.8 ms); the plain local file baseline is much further ahead than DCP.

The worst single WeftFS training step was 71.7 ms versus 14.5 ms and 18.5 ms for the baselines; the checkpoint *submit* path is not that stall (pause max 4.15 ms), so it is host scheduling or background encode contention and is reported, not explained away.
The kill court always loses the steps after the last acked checkpoint; the measured loss is the median steps_lost per scenario, not zero.

A checkpoint in a fresh store completes in 214.6 ms (fresh-store control median 218.3 ms); the second and later checkpoints in the same store take 436.4 ms for the same 4.99 MB container. The per-checkpoint deltas are constant (manifest ~4.59 MB, objects ~0.16 MB, commit ~0.12 MB, advisory index ~62 KB), so the growth is store-state bookkeeping, measured in store_growth_probe and not localised further here.

method.augment_sum_ms: the part of step_sum spent cloning and hashing the state after a checkpoint (harness verification, not training)
method.completion_ms: submit to the save worker's completion callback
method.landing_step: first training step that observes the completed save
method.pause_ms: state clone + async submit on the training thread
method.post_loop_tail_ms: loop wall after the last step: the final in-flight checkpoint has no later step to overlap
method.step_ms: training step wall time including the checkpoint pause on checkpoint steps and the post-checkpoint harness state verification on the next step; medians exclude both of those steps
method.step_sum_ms: sum of every step timer; comparable across configurations because the harness work is identical
method.time_to_safe_resume_ms: SIGKILL epoch to the first completed optimizer step in a fresh process, including store discovery and fresh-process startup
method.wall: loop wall from before step 1 to after the last save completes

non_claims: Single CPU host inside the Docker python court; there is no GPU in the image and no GPU-direct, NCCL, or multi-rank claim.
The dataset is deterministic synthetic next-token data, not a public corpus; the model is a 0.4M-parameter transformer stack, not a production model.
Kill tests are SIGKILL process faults against a local store, not physical media power loss or host-cache loss.
A checkpoint interval shorter than the async completion requires the next checkpoint to wait for the previous save; this court measures that wait but does not claim a queueing policy.
The store is single-writer (MW1); no multi-writer training claim.
torch.save and local DCP are single-host local files; no distributed checkpoint or cloud backend was exercised.
Wall-clock medians are from one host and warm page cache after the first repetition; no fleet or energy claim.
time-to-safe-resume includes fresh-process startup (CPython, the adapter import and torch); the measured store share is the load, and the startup share is reported separately.

resume_exactness.note: Every checkpoint of every normal run was loaded by a separate process. 'probe' is the no-grad next-step loss recorded at snapshot time; 'loss' is the actual next-step loss and the post-step state covers the optimizer step itself.

store_growth_probe.interpretation: A checkpoint in a fresh store has a constant completion; repeated checkpoints in the same store get slower even though the container and the data bytes per checkpoint are constant. The per-commit advisory index segment and the commit record are reported above so the growth can be attributed rather than guessed.

wins: Every one of the 60 checkpoints in the 15 normal runs was restored by a separate process and matched the in-process copy exactly: 60/60 state comparisons, 60/60 next-step loss bits, 45/45 post-step states.
The training thread never runs the encoder: the WeftFS pause is 2.85 ms p50 and 4.15 ms max, and contains only the state clone and the async submit.

Time to safe resume was 1334-1380 ms (p50 per kill scenario, three reps each) and every resumed state was bit-exact. Of that, the checkpoint load is 182.1 ms and store discovery is 28.2-67.4 ms; the rest is fresh-process startup, whose adapter+torch import alone is 848 ms in this court.
WeftFS writes 2.00% fewer physical bytes per checkpoint than torch.save and 6.68% fewer than local DCP (zstd shards and one commit per checkpoint).
All kill scenarios resumed at a complete checkpoint; the store never exposed a partial one, and every resumed state was exact.
